content:
Your values live in one document. The launch date lives in another conversation. The money lives in the budget, and the tasks live on the Gantt chart. A new Launch Team member should not have to open five places to learn where you are and who has the next piece.

A short launch plan answers that. It is optional. You do not need it to move forward, and you should not wait on it. It points to work you already keep. It does not replace that work, and it does not grant permission to launch.

---

## Keep the plan short enough to stay true

Write one or two pages. Name each working document, say where it lives, and name the person who keeps it. Then stop.

Do not paste the values essay, the task list, or the budget onto this page. Those documents change. A copied paragraph does not. When the summary and the source disagree, the source wins. Fix the summary.

<Callout type="warning">
A figure you type into the launch plan is already going stale. Link the first-year budget and the Gantt chart. Do not copy totals, giving projections, salary lines, or task dates into the summary.
</Callout>

The Launch Playbook asks you to tailor a playbook to your own circumstances. This plan is not that playbook. The playbook is the larger set of practices you adapt. The plan is a cover sheet so people can find the current pieces.

---

## Say what this plan refuses to be

Write the limits on the plan itself. The next reader should not have to guess what the page is allowed to do.

| People may treat the plan as | What it actually is |
| --- | --- |
| A fourth commitment document | A pointer. Commitments stay on the three key documents. |
| Proof the church is ready | A map of current documents. Readiness is a leadership judgment, not a page. |
| A network sign-off form | A local summary. A sending church may read it. Reading is not approval. |
| Something Everyfield requires | Optional. Everyfield does not require this plan, score it, or hold a phase for it. |

The Playbook already names the commitment documents. Expectations of a Core Group tell people what membership involves. The Commitment Card is what each member signs. Commitments of a Core Group is what the Senior Pastor or a designated leader signs for the church. None of that moves onto the launch plan. Do not ask anyone to sign it.

<Callout type="important">
Everyfield does not require this plan, and it does not use the plan to judge calling, character, fitness, or spiritual health. A finished plan is not permission to launch. A missing plan is not a block.
</Callout>

---

## Name one owner

The Playbook gives the Launch Coordinator the launch process under the Senior Pastor. That person develops the timeline, tells leaders about deadlines, and chairs the project meetings. Give that same person the launch plan.

The owner keeps the links current, brings the plan to those meetings, and says when a source document changed. Holding the file does not give the coordinator authority over the vision, the date, or the budget. The Senior Pastor still leads.

If you have not named a Launch Coordinator yet, the Senior Pastor holds the file until that person is in place, then hands over the pen. Write that temporary name on the page. An unnamed file looks like shared ownership, which means no ownership.

---

## Point to the five working pieces

The articles below show how to build each piece. The launch plan only records where the current copy lives.

### Values

Link the values document. Link [Defining Your Church Values](/wiki/discovery/defining-your-church-values) if the team still needs the method. Write who last edited the file. Do not restate the values. If it is not written yet, say so and name who will draft it.

### Launch date

Point to [Setting Your Launch Date](/wiki/launch-team/launch-date/setting-your-launch-date). Record the date you are aiming for, the day you chose it, and who can change it. If it is still open, write "not set" and name who will bring the decision. Do not invent a date so the page looks finished.

### Timeline

Point to [Building Your Gantt Chart](/wiki/launch-team/project-management/building-your-gantt-chart). Name the file and its owner. The Playbook recommends that chart for timelines and critical pathways, adjusted to your plant. The chart is the schedule. The plan only says where it is.

### Budget

Point to [First Year Budget Planning](/wiki/administrative/financial/first-year-budget-planning). Name the file and the person who keeps it. Copy no dollar figure. A page people forward should not carry salaries or giving detail.

### Owners

List roles you have actually filled. Start with the Launch Coordinator and the Senior Pastor. Add worship, children, facilities, and money as you name people. Leave a blank for an open role. A guessed name will be treated as an assignment.

---

## Write it in one sitting

Open the five sources and fill the page once. If a source is missing, write that, with a name and a next step. The plan helps when it shows the holes.

- [ ] Title the page as a launch plan, and date the draft
- [ ] Name the owner and the Senior Pastor
- [ ] State where the values document lives
- [ ] Record the launch date, or "not set", and who can change it
- [ ] Link the Gantt chart, with no pasted task list
- [ ] Link the first-year budget, with no copied figures
- [ ] List named owners, and leave blanks for open roles
- [ ] State the review rhythm
- [ ] State that this page is not a commitment document and not a launch approval

```
Launch plan
Draft date:
Owner:
Senior Pastor:
Values: [link]
Last edited by:
Launch date:
[date or not set]
Who can change it:
Gantt chart: [link]
Chart owner:
Budget: [link]
Budget owner:
No figures here.
Worship:
Children:
Facilities:
Review at each
project meeting.
Update the same day
the date, values,
or budget changes.
Not a commitment.
Not launch approval.
```

<Callout type="scripture">
*"Then Yahweh answered me and said, “Write down the vision And write it on tablets distinctly, That the one who reads it may run."* — Habakkuk 2:2 (LSB)
</Callout>

Write it so a teammate can read it and go to the work. Short, current, and pointed at the real documents.

---

## Review it where you already meet

The Launch Coordinator already chairs project meetings so leaders stay informed and work together. Put the launch plan on that agenda. Do not add a meeting whose only job is to approve the summary.

Each time you meet, the owner checks three things. Did the launch date, the values document, or the budget change? Do the links still open the current file? Is any owner line now wrong? Fix what changed before the meeting ends. If nothing changed, say so and move on.

When the launch date moves, update the plan the same day. Two dates in circulation will split the team. Do the same when someone replaces the values document or the budget file. Change the link. Do not paste the new numbers in.

<Callout type="tip">
Add one agenda line: "Launch plan, are the links still current?" If that line turns into editing tasks or money, stop. Open the Gantt chart or the budget. Leave the plan as a pointer.
</Callout>

---

## Mistakes that make the page heavier than the work

**Copying the numbers.** Someone will quote the plan after the budget has moved. Keep the money review in the budget file.

**Collecting signatures.** A signature here blurs the plan with the Commitment Card and with Commitments of a Core Group. For a covenant, use [The Three Key Documents](/wiki/core-group/commitment/the-three-key-documents). Leave this page unsigned.

**Turning it into a gate.** A coach, a sending church, or a network leader may ask to read the plan. Give them the current copy. Comments are counsel, not a sign-off. Everyfield will not treat the page as one either.

**Leaving it ownerless.** Several editors and no name means the page goes stale and nobody notices.

**Polishing the summary while the sources are empty.** A tidy cover sheet over an empty Gantt chart helps no one. If the review keeps finding a missing document, go write that document.
excerpt: How to write an optional launch plan that points to your values, budget, timeline, launch date, and owners, without becoming a commitment or a gate.
title: Writing Your Launch Plan

sources.claim: The Launch Playbook asks each planter to tailor a Launch Playbook to their own circumstances and needs.
sources.quote: Use this as a catalyst for putting together your own Launch Playbook tailored to your circumstances and needs

sources.claim: The Playbook's commitment section names three documents: Expectations of a Core Group, a Commitment Card each Core Group member signs, and Commitments of a Core Group signed by the Senior Pastor or a designated leader.
sources.quote:
#### 1. Expectations of a Core Group
Before people can wholeheartedly commit, they need to know expectations. This document brings clarity and simplicity and helps manage expectations.

#### 2. Commitment Card
Each Core Group Member signs this to bring clarity and simplicity to the process.

#### 3. Commitments of a Core Group
This document lays out expectations for the Core Group. Either the Senior Pastor or designated leader signs on behalf of the Core Group.

sources.claim: The Launch Coordinator owns the launch process under the Senior Pastor, develops the timeline and milestones, keeps leaders informed of deadlines, chairs project meetings, and is charged to bring the launch in on schedule and on budget.
sources.quote:
| **OWN** | Own the launch process under the leadership of the Senior Pastor |
| **LEAD** | Lead the project building a cohesive and coordinated leader team |
| **DEVELOP** | Develop project timeline, milestones and critical pathways |
| **MANAGE** | Manage the timeline, informing leaders of deadlines and keeping on schedule |
| **SCHEDULE** | Schedule and chair project meetings to keep key leaders informed and working together |
| **BRING** | Bring the church launch in on schedule and on budget |

sources.claim: The Playbook recommends starting from a launch project schedule, adjusting it with the Launch Coordinator, and developing a Gantt chart of timelines and critical pathways.
sources.quote:
Use the Launch Project Schedule document as a starting point. Work with your Launch Coordinator to adjust or add items to tailor to your needs.

**Highly recommended:** Develop a Gantt Chart showing project timelines and critical pathways.

rulings: Bryan ruled B15 = Option A: "Optional launch brief" (2026-10-26).
Wording: the title and slug use "launch plan". The backlog title "Writing Your Launch Strategy Document" is a working title and is not used.
Wording: the plan owner is usually the Launch Coordinator. If that role is empty, the Senior Pastor holds the file until a coordinator is named, then hands over the pen.
Wording: the review rhythm is the Launch Coordinator's existing project meeting, plus a same-day link update when the launch date, values document, or budget changes. No new approval meeting.
Wording: this short plan is not the tailored Launch Playbook the Playbook encourages, and it does not replace the three key documents.
Wording: budget figures stay out of the plan so a forwarded summary does not spread salary or giving numbers, and so copied figures cannot drift from the budget file.
Wording: sort_order 5 places this article after the four published articles in launch-team/launch-date.

Wording: sentences that Everyfield does not require, score, or gate this plan restate Bryan's Option A ruling and the house rule that software does not judge calling, character, fitness, or spiritual health. They do not describe a specific screen.
